listenings.text: So, what we do, basically, is we sit in the middle. Your core banking system stays exactly where it is. We do not touch it. On one side you have your core, and on the other side you have the networks, the correspondent banks, the new instant rails, and today every one of those connections is built by hand, one by one, and every one of them breaks in its own way. Our middleware is one layer between the two. You connect once, to us, and we translate the messages into whatever format the other side needs. The typical bank we work with has something like forty point-to-point connections, and after eighteen months it has one. And the part people usually miss, honestly, is reconciliation. Because everything passes through one layer, the matching happens in real time, so your operations team stops spending the morning finding out what happened yesterday.

If you ask me what slows down cross-border payments in Europe, I would not say technology. The technology is mostly there. What slows us down is that every jurisdiction wants to see the same payment in a slightly different way. The same transfer from Frankfurt to Sao Paulo is checked against sanctions lists in Germany, then reported in one format to one regulator and in another format to another, and if one field is missing, the whole thing stops and a person has to look at it. We did a count last year. Around one payment in eight needed a human being somewhere along the way, and almost always for a data problem, not for a real risk. So when people talk about instant payments, I always ask the same question. Instant for whom? The money can move in seconds. The paperwork around it still moves at the speed of the slowest regulator.

Three numbers, and then I will let you get to your coffee. Number one. Ten years ago, a business payment from one continent to another took between two and five days. Today, the majority arrive within an hour, and a large share arrive in minutes. Number two. The cost has not come down anywhere near as fast. For a small business sending a few thousand dollars, the total cost, the fees plus the exchange rate margin, is still several percent, and that is the number that decides whether a small exporter in Brazil or Vietnam can compete at all. Number three, and this is the one I want you to take home. The fastest-growing part of this market is not the big corporates. It is the small and mid-sized companies that were never profitable to serve before. Whoever makes that segment cheap to serve is going to write the next chapter of this industry. That's it. Enjoy the coffee.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to adjust your ear to a voice, an accent or a room until it becomes easy to follow
to say what somebody said again, in your own words, to check it
a word or a structure around a new word that helps you guess what it means
the main idea of what somebody said, without the details
when a speaker begins a sentence, stops, and begins it again differently
to stop following a conversation because you missed one part of it
a conclusion you reach from what you heard, even though nobody said it directly
words like you know or basically that fill time but carry no meaning

paras: Everybody who has been to a big conference knows the feeling. On the first morning, you understand one sentence in three. By the second afternoon, you understand almost everything, and nothing about your English has changed in between. What has changed is that your ear has tuned in: to the accents, to the speed, to the vocabulary of that particular room. The problem is that the meetings that matter most are usually on the first morning.

The good news is that cold listening is a skill, and it has four moves. The first is to stop listening for every word and listen for anchor words instead: the nouns and numbers you already know. In a sentence about settlement, corridors and ninety days, those three words carry most of the meaning, and the rest is grammar and filler phrases like you know and basically, which you can ignore without losing anything.

The second move is to make an inference from the shape of the sentence. If you hear not because of the technology, but because of, you already know the important part is coming next, even if the word after it is new to you. A context clue like that is often more useful than the word itself. The third move is the hardest for careful people: tolerate the gap and keep listening. Speakers repeat themselves, correct themselves, begin with a false start and start the sentence again. If you stop to think about the word you missed, you lose the thread of the next three sentences. If you keep going, the speaker usually fills in the gap for you a few seconds later.

The fourth move is to ask, and to ask well. Sorry, I don't understand tells the other person that everything was lost, so they repeat everything, slowly, and the meeting changes tone. A precise question tells them you got the gist and only need one piece: What was the figure you mentioned? Better still, paraphrase what you think you heard and let them correct you: So you're saying the paperwork is slower than the money? Nobody hears that as a weakness. It sounds like somebody who is listening carefully.

None of this replaces the slow work of exposure, and the best preparation for day one is still twenty minutes a day of real, unscripted speakers with accents that are not American. But on the morning itself, with a coffee in one hand and a stranger talking fast, the four moves are the difference between nodding politely and actually being in the conversation.
